$comment: The retained VM-2 malformed-input corpus. Every entry is a file of artifact bytes plus the
answer verification must give for it.
TWO FIELDS, AND THEY ARE NOT THE SAME FIELD. `expected` is written by a person, beside the
bytes, in FixtureCorpus.cs. `recorded` is what the last regeneration observed. A row pinned
Exact is held to `expected`; a row pinned Recorded is held to `recorded`, which is an
observation under version control rather than an expectation - it cannot prove the answer is
right, and it does prove the answer has not moved without somebody accepting the diff.
Recorded rows exist for the systematic sweeps: truncate the canonical artifact at every
offset, invert every one of its bytes. Hand-computing an answer for each would be a second
implementation of the verifier written by the same hand, which is not an oracle. What every
row is held to regardless of pinning is the closed set: the outcome is one the load stage may
produce, a failure yields no handle, and a success yields one.
Some inverted-byte entries verify successfully, and that is deliberate. A corpus in which
everything fails cannot distinguish a verifier that classifies correctly from one that
rejects whatever it is handed, and the three `control` entries plus those successes are what
make the corpus able to fail in both directions.
PROVENANCE. `Seeded` rows are rewritten from FixtureCorpus.cs whenever the corpus is
regenerated. `Minimized` rows are regressions a fuzz run found and reduced; their bytes are
the artefact, nothing regenerates them, and the writer never rewrites or removes one.
Regenerate with BROILER_CORPUS_WRITE=1 dotnet test Broiler.VM.slnx -c Release. Without the
variable the same code asserts every file, every hash and every answer instead of writing
them.

entries.note: A well-formed artifact. A corpus in which everything fails cannot detect a verifier that rejects everything.
The smallest well-formed artifact that returns a value.
Zero instructions is a well-formed program, not a malformed artifact. Rejecting it would be a verifier inventing a rule.
Zero bytes. The first read is bounded, so this is a truncation and never an index.
One byte, short of the four-byte magic.
The magic and nothing after it: the format version read runs off the end.
A variable-length integer whose continuation bit promises a byte the artifact does not contain.
Byte 0 of the magic inverted. A wrong magic is the profile's own rejection, not a truncation.
Byte 1 of the magic inverted. A wrong magic is the profile's own rejection, not a truncation.
Byte 2 of the magic inverted. A wrong magic is the profile's own rejection, not a truncation.
Byte 3 of the magic inverted. A wrong magic is the profile's own rejection, not a truncation.
The magic in lower case. Matching is over the raw bytes, so it is not a near miss but a miss.
A payload declaring profile-format version 0, which this profile does not know.
A payload declaring profile-format version 2, which this profile does not know.
A payload declaring profile-format version 99, which this profile does not know.
A payload declaring profile-format version 65536, which this profile does not know.
A payload declaring profile-format version 4294967295, which this profile does not know.
Version 1 written with a redundant continuation group. Two encodings of one value would make a byte-identical artifact check meaningless.
Well-formed bytes presented under a descriptor naming a profile-format version the catalog entry does not support. The core answers before the verifier is entered.
Zero sections declared, so neither a constant pool nor code is present.
A constant pool with no code section.
Code with no constant pool.
Nine sections declared and two present: the third section header runs off the end.
A section count above the declared-count ceiling is refused before it can drive a loop.
Sixty-five sections against a sixty-four section ceiling: entering the sixty-fifth is refused.
A section of unknown kind 0. An unknown section is a deterministic rejection, not a skip: skipping would let an artifact carry content nothing looked at.
A section of unknown kind 3. An unknown section is a deterministic rejection, not a skip: skipping would let an artifact carry content nothing looked at.
A section of unknown kind 9. An unknown section is a deterministic rejection, not a skip: skipping would let an artifact carry content nothing looked at.
A section of unknown kind 255. An unknown section is a deterministic rejection, not a skip: skipping would let an artifact carry content nothing looked at.
A section declaring three bytes more than its body. Consuming less than declared is as structural an error as consuming more.
A section declaring one byte less than its body, so the next section header would start inside it.
A section declaring a terabyte inside a twenty-byte artifact. The length is compared with what remains before a frame exists.
A section length of 2^64-1. The comparison is against the remainder, so the arithmetic never has to hold the sum.
Four billion constants declared. The count is refused before anything proportional to it is allocated, which is the ordering the whole guard exists for.
One more than the declared-count ceiling. The interesting case is the boundary, not the absurd number.

Exactly at the declared-count ceiling, so the count is admitted and the pool is allocated - and then the artifact runs out of bytes long before it has 65,536 values. Resource-hostile and in bounds at once.
Three constants declared and two present, so the third is read out of the next section's header and the frame no longer closes where it said it would.
A constant encoded with a redundant continuation group.
A constant whose encoding carries more groups than sixty-four bits can hold.
A code length above the declared-count ceiling.
Sixty-four bytes of code declared and one present.
An opcode outside the fixture's instruction set. Nothing unverified may be reachable by the executor.
An instruction whose operand byte is not there.
A constant index past the end of a pool of one.
An index exactly one past a pool of two. Off-by-one is the case an index check is most likely to get wrong.
Well-formed bytes presented under a descriptor that tightens the artifact-bytes ceiling below their own length. The refusal happens before the first byte is read.
The same artifact under a request of zero. A ceiling of nothing admits nothing, which is what a bound of zero has to mean.
